## Design

### 2026-10-09 – October 9: Drew the whole schematic for my Starbie in KiCad

**6h**

October 9: Drew the whole schematic for my Starbie in KiCad

Today I started my Starbie, a little desk pet with a screen that reacts when you tilt it, shake it, or press its buttons. I had never used KiCad before, so I followed the [Week 1 Starbie guide](https://github.com/SharKingStudios/Starbie) step by step. First I installed the care package (the extra symbol and footprint libraries the guide provides), then I made a new KiCad project and worked through the "Schematic Editor" part of the guide.

Following the guide, I drew the full schematic (the wiring diagram of the board). It has:

- A XIAO ESP32-C3 as the brain
- An OLED screen (J1)
- An MPU6050 motion sensor (J2) so it can feel tilting and shaking
- A DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor (U3), with a 10k pull-up resistor (R1) on its data wire
- Two push buttons (SW1 and SW2)

How I wired it:  Like the guide shows, I used net labels (the L key) instead of drawing long wires everywhere. Pins with the same label are connected, like name tags. D1 goes to the DHT11 data pin, D2 to button 1, D3 to button 2, D4 to SDA, and D5 to SCL. The OLED and the MPU6050 share the same two I2C wires (SDA and SCL). Every part also gets +3.3V and GND for power, and the buttons connect to GND on their other side.

What went wrong:  At first I had SDA and SCL swapped on pins D4 and D5. The guide's firmware expects D4 to be SDA and D5 to be SCL, so my screen and motion sensor would not have worked. I caught it when I checked my schematic against the pin table in the guide, and fixed it by renaming the two labels. I also put no-connect flags (the X marks) on the pins I'm not using so KiCad knows I left them empty on purpose.

Next:  follow the guide's next steps: assign footprints to every part, then place and route the actual PCB.
